title: The rivers and the sea
hookLine: rivers rise from the sea and run back to it: where we come from, and where we go
carry: we come from Being, and go back
tomorrow: the tree: cut it, it bleeds
last: MADHU — ONE BEING UNDER EVERY NAME.

cards: Rivers have names, and people love those names. They write songs about them, fight over them, scatter ashes in them, bathe in them on holy days. The Ganga, the Yamuna, the Mississippi, the Thames.
A river has a source, a path, a personality: slow and brown, or fast and cold. Then it reaches the sea. Stand on a beach and look out.
Which part of that water was the Ganga? Uddalaka asks his son the same thing.

teach.h: EAST AND WEST, FROM SEA TO SEA.
teach.b: These rivers, my dear, Uddalaka says, the eastern ones flow toward the east, the western ones toward the west. They go from sea to sea. They become the sea itself.

teach.h: THEY DON'T KNOW: I AM THIS RIVER.
teach.b: And there, in the sea, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Notice that little phrase, from sea to sea.

Commentators hear the water cycle in it: water rises from the sea as cloud, falls as rain, gathers into rivers, and runs back home. The river was the sea all along, on a long walk. Then he turns it around.
In the same way, my dear, all these creatures, though they have come from Being, don't know: we have come from Being.

teach.h: EVERYTHING COMES FROM BEING, AND GOES BACK.
teach.b: Here is the teaching, and it runs all through Hinduism: everything comes out of Being, the one reality later teachers call Brahman, and everything goes back to it.
A life is a river, truly itself while it runs, and never cut off from the sea it came from. And Uddalaka says again, whatever they are here, tiger or lion or gnat, they become that.
Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world; you are that, Shvetaketu. Some Vedanta schools hear the river as finally nothing but sea.
Others hear it as a real, beloved part of the sea. Either way, when someone you love is near the end, this teaching doesn't say they'll vanish. It says the river is going home.

how: Rivers are sacred for many Hindus, who bathe in them on festival days and immerse ashes after cremation; Vedanta teachers often use Uddalaka's rivers and the sea to describe the relation of the self to Brahman.

o: a holy river where pilgrims bathe on feast days
the churning that brought up the gods' nectar
the sea, where the rivers lose their names

games.q: what's inside the lesson — tap the pairs.
p: the river starts and ends as ocean
don't know they came from Being

s: Uddalaka says the rivers start from the sea too
they go from sea to sea: rising as cloud, falling as rain, running home.
in this lesson, a tiger stops being a tiger
whatever they are here, tiger or gnat, they become that; the river is truly a river while it runs.
Vedanta schools all read the rivers and sea the same way
some hear the river as finally only sea; others as a real part of the sea.

games.q: if the river becomes the sea, was the river ever real? by Uddalaka's lesson, what fits?
o: no: only the sea was ever real, so the river never mattered.
yes: truly a river while it runs, and the sea all along. Vedanta schools weigh the two differently.
the river and the sea have nothing to do with each other.
games.why: the river runs from sea to sea, and whatever creatures are here, they truly are. some schools stress the sea, others the beloved river.

practice: Picture a river you know and start at its source, a spring in the hills; on each breath, let it run a little farther, past towns and under bridges, wider and slower.
Then let it reach the sea, and rest in the open water without needing to know which part was which.

wordCard.voice: Samudra, the sea, the gathering of waters. Rivers flow from sea to sea, become the sea, and there don't say I am this river; so creatures come from Being and don't know it.

orig.note: Sanskrit samudra: the sea, the gathering of waters. the rivers go from samudra to samudra.

carryVoice: Your line: we come from Being, and go back. Every river was on its way home. Day three hundred forty-six, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.10.1–3 (the rivers and the sea; the refrain)
Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.8; Prashna Upanishad 6.5 (rivers losing name and form)
